code.description: The program, in the dialect the system prompt describes. Print anything you need to see.

content.content:
## Code mode

You have exactly one tool, `eval`, which runs the body of an async JavaScript function against
this workspace and returns whatever that code printed. Nothing else is visible to you: a value
you do not `print` never reaches you. Do not use `import` or `require` — the API below is
in scope.

Prefer one `eval` call that does the whole job — query, inspect, change, print — over a call
per step. Print the specific values you need to reason about, not whole objects, and keep the
output small.

### API

- `print(...values)` — adds a line to this call's output. Strings go through verbatim,
  everything else is printed as JSON.
- `await query(typename, props?)` — objects of that typename, optionally narrowed by exact
  property values, e.g. `await query('example.com/type/Task', { status: 'open' })`.
- `await make(typename, props)` — a new object; it is not stored until you add it.
- `await add(obj)` / `await remove(obj)` — store or delete an object.
- `update(obj, (obj) => { obj.field = value; })` — the only way to change a stored object.
- `await flush()` — waits for pending writes to land; call it before printing a final
  confirmation.
- `ref(obj)` — a reference to an object you hold. A `Ref<typename>` field takes one, never
  an id or a URI string: `await make('example.com/type/Task', { title: 'Review', owner: ref(person) })`.
  Where an operation's input takes references, pass `ref(obj)` too.

### Types

Every registered type and its fields (`?` marks an optional field). This is the whole schema —
do not introspect it further. A `Ref<typename>` field holds a reference to another object, not
the object or its id.

- `com.example.type.expando` — 
- `com.example.type.task` — title: string, status: string, priority?: number
- `org.dxos.type.feed` — name?: string, kind?: string, namespace?: "data" | "trace", rewindFrom?: string
- `org.dxos.type.skill` — name: string, description?: string, instructions: object, tools: string[], agentCanEnable?: boolean, mcpServers?: object[], hooks?: object[]
- `org.dxos.type.instructions` — name?: string, description?: string, input: object, output: object, text: Ref<org.dxos.type.text>, skills: Ref<org.dxos.type.skill>[], objects?: Ref<org.dxos.schema.anyObject>[], commands?: object[]
- `org.dxos.type.function` — name: string, description?: string, updated?: string, source?: Ref<org.dxos.schema.anyObject>, inputSchema?: object, outputSchema?: object, services?: string[], binding?: string, icon?: string
- `org.dxos.type.assistant.chat` — name?: string, viewType?: string, remote?: boolean, feed: Ref<org.dxos.type.feed>, instructions?: Ref<org.dxos.type.instructions>, model?: Ref<org.dxos.schema.anyObject>, tasks: Ref<org.dxos.type.task>[]
- `org.dxos.type.trigger` — runnable?: Ref<org.dxos.type.function>, spec?: object, enabled?: boolean, remote?: boolean, concurrency?: number, inputNodeId?: string, input?: object
- `org.dxos.type.tag` — label: string, hue?: string
- `org.dxos.type.alarm` — wakeAt: number, message?: string, created: string
- `org.dxos.type.view` — query: object, projection: object

### Operations

The skills above describe their capabilities as tools; in code mode they are NOT tools. Each one
is an async function on `ops`, taking one argument matching its parameter schema. A failed
operation throws, so wrap a call you expect to fail in `try`/`catch`. The names are kebab-case,
so they are indexed rather than dotted.

- `await ops["com-example-operation-score"](input)` — Scores a task title for urgency. Returns the title's length as the score.
  input: {"type":"object","properties":{"title":{"type":"string","description":"The title to score"}},"required":["title"],"additionalProperties":false}
